title: Moving gold out of New York is a poor signal of a reserve manager’s dollar allocation
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: A central bank can move physical gold out of the United States and retain a large allocation to dollar assets. Colin Weiss documents four episodes involving Germany, France and the Netherlands in which the dollar continued to dominate foreign exchange reserves after a transfer of gold. For interpreting reserve-manager behaviour, the distinction concerns two decisions with different denominators. Moving a bar changes the jurisdiction where it is held. The reported dollar share is the fraction of foreign exchange reserves invested in dollar assets. A transfer of gold gives no mechanical reason for this second measure to change.

Both decisions could nevertheless reflect a common consideration. Gold held within the reach of a sanctioning government may be difficult to access. Domestic custody can provide protection against that particular risk, though the paper’s footnotes also point to constraints on dealing in sanctioned gold. Location matters for access to markets as well. Russia’s accumulation of domestically held gold and reduction of dollar holdings, and Turkey’s 2018 repatriation alongside a cut in the dollar share, illustrate circumstances in which the two choices did move together. In the European cases, official statements about the transfers did not identify sanctions or expropriation as key motives (discussion of custody and footnotes 2–4). The paper does not estimate the motives of individual reserve managers from their reported holdings.

Germany moved about one-fifth of the gold it had held in the United States to domestic vaults between 2013 and 2017. Its dollar share stayed around 90% over that period and remained above 80% at the latest observation. The Netherlands moved roughly two-fifths of its US-custodied gold home in 2014, when the dollar share was about 83%. It subsequently fell towards 50% in 2018, then recovered. The timing matters. The Dutch central bank hedges currency exposure, and its 2016 annual report cited the cost of hedging as a reason to reduce dollar exposure that year. Weiss treats changing hedged returns as a possible explanation for part of the later variation; subsequent reports did not supply the same explanation (Figure 1a–b and footnotes 5–6).

France moved all of its remaining US-held gold home in 2025 and early 2026. Its dollar share stayed near 60% in the annual data shown for 2024 and 2025, having fallen in 2023. Weiss relates that earlier fall to sales generating income during a period of rising net interest expense. For the Netherlands in 2026, there was a decline alongside a transfer: the authorities moved two-fifths of US-held gold to London and the monthly series showed a drop of roughly ten percentage points in the dollar share. London was a change of foreign custodian. The dollar still accounted for the majority of FX reserves. The monthly series used here runs below the Dutch annual-report series in recent years, so splicing the two charts would create a misleading impression of the timing and scale of diversification (Figure 1c–d and footnotes 7–8).

The cases support a narrow inference for a portfolio manager. A custody announcement alone provides little basis for revising an estimate of dollar-asset demand by these institutions. Changes in portfolio allocation, currency hedging, income generation and access to bullion markets can occur on different dates and for different reasons. The note offers descriptive comparisons for selected publicised transfers. It provides neither a forecast of future reserve flows nor an estimate of the exchange-rate effect of a given transaction.

questions.question: Can actual purchases and sales be separated from changes in reported portfolio shares?
questions.detail: The charts track fractions of reserves, with different reporting frequencies and incomplete overlap around recent transfers. An FX flow estimate needs to distinguish transactions from valuation and denominator changes. Reconcile same-date stock and transaction disclosures in central-bank annual reports and the foreign currency liquidity returns used in the note. Flag periods for which the published information cannot support that reconciliation.

questions.question: How much dollar exposure remains after currency hedging?
questions.detail: The Netherlands reports active currency-risk management, and its 2016 report attributes part of an adjustment to hedging costs. Gross dollar holdings and net exposure can give different signals for underlying FX demand. Look for forward positions, hedge ratios and the accounting treatment of derivatives in reserve-management reports. Compare hedged returns with the bank’s stated explanation before generalising that episode.

questions.question: Which features would make a custody transfer more informative about strategic reallocation?
questions.detail: The European cases differ from the Russian and Turkish episodes in stated motivations and accompanying allocations. The case selection cannot tell us how often either pattern occurs. Review dated official custody decisions, the destination of the metal, stated tradability objectives and subsequent disclosed FX composition across a broader set of transfers. Such evidence would help distinguish an operational move from a change in currency preference.
